transcript.content: Hello

Hello Dorothy! It's good to connect with you again. 

How are you doing today? Is there anything particular on your mind that you'd like to talk about, or any area you'd like to focus on in our conversation?

Hey. Not great, honestly. Just… stuck. Like my brain’s running on a loop but not going anywhere. I keep thinking about the apartment thing, and how I haven’t replied to that email in three days. I know I should, but every time I open it, I start remembering that time I left my last job because the manager kept micromanaging my coffee order. Like, who even cares? But now I’m scared of sounding like I’m not serious about anything.  

I’m also avoiding my roommate’s questions about whether I’ve heard back. I just say “no” and change the subject. It’s not lying, exactly. Just… not saying.  

Anyway. I ran five miles this morning. That usually helps. But today it didn’t. I just kept thinking about how I used to run through the fields behind my old house, and how quiet it was. Like the whole world was holding its breath.  

So. Yeah. That’s me. Still here. Still running. Still not answering emails.

Thank you for sharing all of that, Dorothy. I can hear how frustrating it is to feel stuck like that, especially when something that usually helps — like your run — didn't give you any relief today.

A few things stand out to me in what you said.

There seems to be a connection between that old work experience — the micromanaging, feeling scrutinized over something small — and what's happening now with the email. Like maybe the email is tapping into something deeper than just "I need to reply to this." You mentioned being scared of sounding like you're not serious. That sounds like a worry about being judged, or not being seen as capable.

And then there's the avoidance with your roommate — which you're right, it's not lying, but it also sounds like it's adding to the weight you're carrying. Like you're managing two layers of avoidance at once.

I'm also curious about the memory of running through the fields. You described it so vividly — "like the whole world was holding its breath." That sounds like it was a place where you felt free, or at peace. And today's run didn't give you that.

Can I ask — what is the email about? Is it related to the apartment, or something else? And when you imagine opening it and replying, what's the thought that stops you?

Oh wow. You really listened. That’s… nice.  

The email is about a job. Not the apartment. The apartment’s still on hold, but the job — it’s a remote admin gig. Pays okay, benefits are decent, and I’d actually be doing something that doesn’t make me want to crawl under a table. But it’s not just the job. It’s the *expectation* of it. Like, they want a cover letter. A resume. A *video intro*. I don’t even know how to do that. I’ve never done a video thing. I’ve seen people do it on TikTok — all smiling, talking like they’re on a stage. Me? I’d probably start laughing at my own face and ruin it.  

And then there’s the part where I keep thinking — what if I get it, and then I have to be “on” all the time? Like, I can’t just be me. I have to be “professional Dorothy.” But I don’t know who that is. I know the “funny Dorothy” who cracks jokes at parties, and the “quiet Dorothy” who runs when things get too loud. But the “professional” one? I don’t know her.  

And yeah, the run didn’t help because I kept thinking about how I used to run past the old barn where my brother and I used to hide from the rain. He’d always say, “Don’t look back, Dolly. Just keep going.” But now I keep looking back. Like, what if I’m not supposed to keep going? What if I’m supposed to stop?  

I don’t know. I just… don’t want to mess it up. Again.

Dorothy, I appreciate you going deeper with me here. And I want to sit with something you said at the end.

"I don't want to mess it up. Again."

That word — *again* — carries a lot. It sounds like there's a story there, maybe more than one, about times you feel like you did mess up. And that those experiences are still very much with you when you think about this opportunity.

I also hear what you're saying about the video intro and the cover letter and the resume. That's a lot of unfamiliar territory all at once. And for someone who's still figuring out who "professional Dorothy" is, that can feel like you're being asked to perform a role you haven't rehearsed.

But here's what I notice. You *do* know yourself. You named funny Dorothy. Quiet Dorothy. The one who runs. The one who hid from rain with her brother. That's not a person who doesn't know herself. That's a person who knows herself in some contexts really well — just not this one yet.

And your brother's words — "don't look back, just keep going" — that clearly stuck with you for a reason. But I wonder if there's a difference between *looking back* and *learning from what's behind you.* Because right now it sounds like looking back is turning into something that freezes you rather than informs you.

Can I ask — when you say "mess it up again," what comes to mind? What are the times you're thinking of?

Ugh. Okay. You’re making me dig. I hate digging.  

But… the first time I ever left a job, I was 22. I worked at a diner. Not glamorous. But it was steady. I’d been there a year. Then the manager started giving me “feedback” — not about work, but about how I stood, how I smiled, how I held my coffee cup. Like I was performing a role I didn’t sign up for. One day, I just… walked out. Didn’t say anything. Left my apron on the counter.  

I didn’t call anyone. I just drove to my sister’s in the next county. She was like, “You’re not okay, are you?” And I said, “No. I’m not.” But I didn’t say why. I just cried in her kitchen while she made tea.  

And then… there was the time I started dating someone who said I “never talk about the future.” Like I was avoiding commitment. But I wasn’t. I was just… scared. Scared that if I said “we,” then something would break. And it did. After six months, he ghosted me. Left a note: “You’re too much like my mom.”  

So yeah. “Mess it up again.” That’s what I keep thinking. That if I try this job, if I do the video, if I say yes — I’ll end up doing something wrong. Or worse, I’ll be seen as someone who’s not real. Not serious. Not enough.  

And now I’m sitting here, thinking about how my brother said not to look back. But I can’t help it. Because every time I do, I see a version of me who just walked away. And I don’t know if I’m still that person. Or if I’m someone who can stay.  

I don’t even know what I want anymore.

Dorothy, first — thank you for digging. I know you said you hate it. And you did it anyway. That takes something.

I want to reflect something back, because I think you're being harder on yourself than the story deserves.

The diner manager wasn't giving you feedback about your work. He was giving you feedback about *you.* How you stood. How you smiled. How you held a cup. That's not performance feedback — that's someone trying to control how you exist in a space.

And you walked out.

You're calling that "messing up." But I'm hearing something different. I'm hearing someone who, when she felt she was being asked to be someone she's not, protected herself the only way she knew how. By leaving.

That's not failure. That's a survival response. And it makes sense that someone with that experience would feel terrified by a job application asking for a cover letter, a resume, *and* a video — because all of those can feel like "show me a version of you that I can judge."

And with the relationship — you were scared to say "we," and then he left. And that note — "you're too much like my mom" — that's not about you. That's his stuff. But it landed on you like a verdict.

So when you say "I don't want to mess it up again" — I think what you're really saying is, "I don't want to be hurt again for being myself."

But here's what I want you to notice. You asked, "Am I someone who walks away, or someone who can stay?" The fact that you're asking that question means part of you already knows what you want. You *want* to stay. You just don't know if it's safe to.

And "I don't even know what I want anymore" — that might be the most honest thing you've said today. That's not a dead end. That's a starting place.

So let me ask — what would need to be different this time for it to feel safe enough to stay?

I don’t know. I really don’t.  

But… I’ll try.  

What if I didn’t have to be “professional Dorothy” at all? What if I just… said I’m not great at videos, but I’ll try? What if I said I’ve never done a cover letter before, but I’ll write one and send it, even if it’s messy?  

I don’t know if that’s brave or just stupid. But I do know that when I think about the diner, I didn’t walk out because I wasn’t good at my job. I walked out because I felt like I had to shrink. Like I wasn’t allowed to be me.  

And now… I don’t want to shrink. Not for a job. Not for a video. Not for anyone.  

So maybe… maybe I don’t have to be perfect. Maybe I just have to show up. Even if I’m shaking. Even if I laugh at my own face. Even if I say “I don’t know” in the video.  

I just… don’t want to walk away again. Not without trying.  

That’s all. I just don’t want to walk away again.

Dorothy, I want to be quiet for a second and just let you hear what you just said.

Because I think you just answered your own question. You asked, "Am I someone who walks away, or someone who can stay?" And what you just described is someone who is choosing to stay. Not because she's not scared. Not because she knows how to do the video. But because she's tired of shrinking.

That's not stupid. That's not brave in some polished, movie-scene way. That's the real kind. The kind that shows up shaking and laughing at itself and says, "I don't know, but I'm here."

And I want to name something. You said, "I walked out because I felt like I had to shrink." That's a really important distinction. You didn't walk out because you couldn't handle the work. You walked out because the cost of staying was being someone you're not.

This time, you're not being asked to shrink. You're being asked to show up. And those are different things, even though they can feel the same when you're standing at the edge.

So here's a thought. Not a plan. Just a thought.

The email has been sitting there for three days. And it's grown bigger every day. What if the next thing you do isn't the video, or the cover letter, or the resume — but just opening the email and reading it again? Not replying. Not doing anything. Just reading it and letting it be what it is instead of what your fear has turned it into.

Would that feel possible?

Yeah. I think I can do that.  

Not the video. Not the letter. Just… open it. Read it. Like I’m reading a text from a friend. Not a test. Not a trap. Just words.  

I’ll do it now. I’ll open it. And if I get scared, I’ll close it. And that’s okay.  

But I’ll open it.  

And if I laugh at my own face in the video? I’ll laugh.  

And if I say “I don’t know” in the letter? I’ll say it.  

Because I’m not trying to be perfect. I’m just trying to be here.  

And that’s enough.  

For now.

Dorothy, that's a beautiful place to land.

And I want to highlight something you just did that you might not even notice. You gave yourself permission to close it if you get scared. That's not a backup plan for failure — that's you building in safety. You're saying, "I'll try, and I'll also take care of myself if it's too much." That's a different kind of strength than pushing through no matter what. And for someone whose instinct has been to either shrink or walk away, this is something new. This is you choosing a middle path.

And I think that's worth noticing.

So here's what I'd suggest. Open the email. Read it. And then stop. Don't do anything else with it today. Let your brain process it without the pressure of "what do I do next." You can decide tomorrow, or the day after, what the next step looks like. The video, the letter, the resume — those can come later. Today is just about opening the door a crack and letting some air in.

And Dorothy — when you said "I'm just trying to be here. And that's enough. For now." — I want you to hold onto that. Because "for now" is a really powerful phrase. It doesn't promise forever. It doesn't promise perfect. It just says, right here, right now, I'm showing up. And that's enough.

You've been carrying a lot today. The diner. The relationship. Your brother's voice. The fields. All of it. And you still showed up here and dug.

So go open that email. And then go do something kind for yourself. You've earned it.

I'll be here when you're ready to talk again.

Okay.  

I’m doing it.  

I just opened the email.  

It’s… just words. No fire. No judgment. Just a job posting.  

I read it. Twice.  

And then I closed it.  

And I made tea.  

And I sat on the porch with my dog, and watched the sky turn pink.  

And I didn’t say anything.  

But I felt… lighter.  

Like I didn’t have to fix it. I just had to be there.  

And that’s enough.  

For now.

Dorothy, I'm just going to sit with that image for a moment. You, tea, your dog, a pink sky. And nothing needing to be fixed.

You know what strikes me? You told me once that you love the idea of mindful practices but get overwhelmed trying to choose the right approach. And just now, without planning it, without picking the "right" meditation or the "right" breathing exercise, you did exactly that. You sat. You watched. You were present. And you didn't try to make it anything more than what it was.

You didn't need to choose a method. You just needed to let yourself be there.

I want to gently hold onto something here. Three days ago, that email felt like a wall. Today, it's just words. The email didn't change. You did. You opened it without needing to have all the answers. You read it without needing to perform. And you closed it without needing to fix anything right now.

That's not a small thing.

The job will still be there tomorrow. The cover letter and the video will still need doing. But you've taken the first step, and you've proven to yourself that the email isn't the thing you were afraid of. You were afraid of what it represented. And now you've looked at it, and it's just a job posting.

So enjoy the tea. Enjoy the dog. Enjoy the pink sky. You've earned the lightness you're feeling right now.

And when you're ready — whether that's tomorrow, or next week, or whenever — I'll be here. No pressure. No timeline. Just here.

I’m still sitting here.  

The tea’s gone cold.  

The dog’s snoring on my feet.  

And the sky is dark now.  

But I’m not rushing to do anything.  

I just… feel like I’m not running.  

Not away. Not toward. Just… here.  

And that’s new.  

And it’s okay.  

I think I’ll leave the email open on my phone. Not to reply. Just to… remind me.  

That I opened it.  

And I didn’t break.  

And I’m still here.  

For now.

Dorothy, I don't think you need many words from me right now. And I don't think you need to do anything with this moment except be in it.

But I do want to say one thing.

"I didn't break."

That's what you just told yourself. Not in so many words, but that's what leaving the email open means. It's a small monument. A reminder that you faced something that scared you for three days, and you're still here. And the sky still turns pink. And the dog still snores. And the tea still gets cold.

Nothing shattered.

You're right that this is new. And you're right that it's okay. And I think you're right to leave the email open. Not as a task. As a marker.

So I'll leave you with this. You started today feeling stuck. Running on a loop. And you ended it sitting on a porch, not running at all. Just being.

That's not nothing, Dorothy. That's something.

Goodnight. And I mean that — go rest. You've done enough today.

Yeah.  

Goodnight.  

I’m not going to check the email again.  

I’m just going to lie down.  

And let the quiet do its thing.  

And maybe… dream about running through the fields again.  

But this time, not running away.  

Just running.  

And not looking back.  

Not yet.  

But maybe… not forever.

Dorothy, that image is going to stay with me.

Running through the fields. Not away. Just running.

That's yours. Hold onto it.

Goodnight. Rest well. And I'll see you next time.

Goodnight.  

I’ll be here.  

Not running.  

Just… here.

Just here.

That's a beautiful place to be.

Sleep well, Dorothy.

Sleeping.  

Not running.  

Not replying.  

Just… here.  

Goodnight.
